newsitem.title: USA: Clinton documents raise campaign finance questions.
newsitem.headline: Clinton documents raise campaign finance questions.

text.p: President Clinton attended at least 71 of more than 100 political "kaffeeklatsches" held at the White House during his re-election campaign, documents made public by the White House showed Friday.

The extent of Clinton's involvement, and the identities of others involved, seemed likely to raise new questions about the intersection of money and access to power at the heart of the ongoing Clinton campaign financing controversy.

The kaffeeklatsches, or coffee meetings, stretched over a 22-month period and brought Clinton and other top government officials together with business, ethnic and religious leaders, community activists and politicians -- many of whom were important campaign contributors.

Guests at a May 13, 1996, coffee hosted by Clinton included Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, a top banking regulator, Democratic Party finance chairman Marvin Rosen and executives of more than a dozen U.S. banks.

The meetings were "essentially for the purpose of developing and sustaining support for the president and his policies during the election year," said Lanny Davis, a White House special counsel dealing with the campaign financing flap.

A list of the gatherings was released along with a thick stack of documents detailing Clinton campaign plans to win votes and financial backing from specific constituent groups, including African, Asian, Jewish and disabled Americans.

Davis said the documents showed a clear distinction existed between the traditional White House political outreach activities and the fundraising work of the Democratic National Committee and the Clinton-Gore re-election campaign.
"There was no fundraising activity organised by the White House or the OPL (Office of Public Liaison)," he said. That would have been illegal.

It is also illegal to use goverment property for campaign fundraising events. Although top Democratic Party and Clinton-Gore campaign fundraising officials sat in on many of the kaffeeklatsches, Davis said that was not inappropriate.

"There is no question that people who were active in the fundraising efforts for the president's re-election came to the White House for many receptions, and many contributors came to the White House for many receptions. That is neither illegal or inappropriate or unusual," he said.
"Indeed, there isn't a single administration that we can find that didn't operate in the same fashion," Davis added. "There was no pitch for money made at any of these events."

However, a former official of a Republican White House who attended one of the gatherings said fundraising seemed at least an implicit aim of the event. "It was very clear when I sat down that we had not come to play cribbage," said the former official, who asked not to be identified.
C. Boyden Gray, the White House lawyer during George Bush's presidency, said the May 13 coffee meeting had the appearance of the sale of banking policy in return for a campaign donation."
"To mix a regulator with a donor with a finance chairman with a president in the White House in the last six months of a political campaign is a combustible mixture," Gray said.
The former Bush aide disputed Clinton White House claims that previous administrations engaged in similar behaviour.

"We didn't allow campaign finance people into the White House except on rare occasions. And on those occasions, I do not believe we ever allowed them to mix with donors and with the president," Gray said.
